title: ⚔️ Chapter boss ⭐⭐⭐: reading between the words

questions.prompt: Rewrite with a phrasal verb: "Being extremely busy, the boss delayed her trip abroad several times." Which sentence says the same thing?

options.text: The boss put aside her trip abroad several times.
The boss put forward her trip abroad several times.
The boss put away her trip abroad several times.
The boss put off her trip abroad several times.

questions.explanation: To put something off is to postpone it, to defer it, to reschedule it for later — precisely what a boss too busy to travel keeps doing. To put aside and to put away both mean to save something or to store it away, and to put forward means to suggest or to propose, as in to put forward a theory. The verb is the same in all four sentences; the particle alone changes the meaning completely, which is why a phrasal verb has to be learnt as one single item.

questions.prompt: Match each idiomatic expression with what it really means.

options.text: You could hear a pin drop.
He is the life and soul of the party.
She made it to the top.
Everything has gone well up to now.
He is the most amusing person there.

questions.explanation: So far, so good says that things have gone well up to now and promises nothing at all about the rest. You could hear a pin drop describes a place so quiet that even the tiniest sound would be heard. The life and soul of the party is the person who makes the party fun for everybody else. And to make it to the top is to become successful, to reach the highest position. Not one of the four can be worked out from its individual words, which is the very definition of an idiom — and the reason a good dictionary lists idioms under a heading of their own.

questions.prompt: Read this short text printed on a small box: "Keep out of the reach of children. Do not use after the date printed on the side of the box. If the cough lasts more than five days, consult your doctor or your pharmacist." What text type is it, and what is its field?

options.text: A description of an item — hygiene

questions.explanation: Warnings, an expiry date and the advice to consult a doctor or a pharmacist are the signals of instructions for use printed on a medicine, exactly like the lozenge notice in the book. An advertisement would praise the product to make you buy it, a store receipt would show what was paid and how the goods can be exchanged, and a description of an item would tell you what the product is made of and what it does. Naming a text type means reading its signals first, and its subject afterwards.

questions.prompt: Check ALL the pairs whose two words are pronounced exactly the same.
questions.explanation: Flour and flower, higher and hire, some and sum are homophones: different spellings, different meanings, one single sound — like one and won, sea and see, I and eye. The other two pairs only look alike on the page. Thought is simply though plus a letter on the page, yet the two share neither their first consonant nor their vowel, and thought ends on a /t/ that though does not have; lose ends with the /z/ sound while loose ends with /s/. Only the ear decides here, and the spelling is precisely the thing that changes.

questions.prompt: In Britain, four neighbours are talking about tea. Which sentence expresses a desire — not a suggestion and not a request?

options.text: Make us a cuppa, will you?

questions.explanation: I'm dying for a cuppa says how badly the speaker wants the tea and asks nobody to do anything, so it expresses a desire. Shall we…? and Would you like…? both put an idea to the other person, which makes them suggestions, while Make us a cuppa, will you? asks somebody to act, which makes it a request. Notice the word itself, too: cuppa belongs to colloquial English, and a cup of tea is the form you would write in an essay.

questions.prompt: A report says that people in Britain drink about 200 000 000 cups of tea a day. How is that figure read aloud, and how is it written with commas?
questions.explanation: Each space, or each comma, sets off a group of three digits: 200 000 reads two hundred thousand, and 200 000 000, which has two groups after the first, reads two hundred million. When a number stands in front of them, million, billion and trillion take no -s and are followed by a plural noun — two hundred million cups, a billion people. The -s only comes back when no number precedes, as in millions of cups.
